name: Mistletoe extract
lead: Mistletoe extract is prepared from European mistletoe (Viscum album), a semi-parasitic plant. Standardised or proprietary extracts such as Iscador have been used as complementary cancer treatments, mainly in German-speaking countries, and the plant also appears as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare products.[1][2]

The plant's toxins include viscumin, which inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis by a mechanism similar to ricin's; European mistletoe is described as more toxic than American mistletoe.[3] Medicinal extracts contain mistletoe lectins that have been studied for immune-stimulating effects.[2][4]
Published human research concerns cancer patients, not skin. No study of mistletoe extract on skin or appearance was identified in the sources reviewed.

paras: A 1989 study reported that the beta-galactoside-specific lectin from Iscador had immunomodulatory effects in rabbits and patients.[2] A 1990 study reported that the lectin increased secretion of tumour necrosis factor alpha and interleukins 1 and 6 by human mononuclear cells.[4] The lectin's ligand-binding characteristics have also been characterised.[5]

Human studies relate to cancer. The EORTC 18871/DKG 80-1 phase III melanoma trial included an Iscador M arm alongside interferon arms and an observation group.[6] A randomised trial in China examined quality of life with a standardised extract in breast, ovarian and lung cancer,[7] and a placebo-controlled trial reported improved quality of life in breast cancer patients during chemotherapy with extract PS76A2.[8] A randomised trial examined quality of life in advanced pancreatic cancer,[9] and a 2009 systematic review examined survival in patients given Iscador.[10] A trial in resected head and neck cancer has also been published.[11] No trial examined skin or cosmetic outcomes.
Wikipedia describes viscumin as toxic and notes that the plant's historical medicinal and folk uses are varied.[3]

timeline.event: Study reports immunomodulatory effects of the Iscador lectin.[2]
EORTC phase III melanoma trial results published.[6]

card.summary: A mistletoe botanical used in some skincare; its research is in cancer care, not skin.
card.note: Plant toxins (viscumin) are documented; no skin trials found.

quick.overview:
Mistletoe extract comes from Viscum album. Injectable extracts such as Iscador have been used as complementary cancer treatments, and the plant appears as a botanical in some skincare.

Human trials examine cancer patients; none examine skin or appearance.
quick.mechanism: Mistletoe lectins have been reported in laboratory and patient studies to stimulate immune signalling such as TNF-alpha and interleukins.
quick.risks: The plant contains the toxin viscumin, which Wikipedia says works like ricin. Topical cosmetic safety was not covered in the reviewed sources.
